raw_case_text:
Patient 2 was a 3-year-old girl who presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and retroorbital headache. There had been one episode of gum bleeding on the first day of illness. She had been apparently a well child without any significant illnesses in the past. WBC count done on day 2, on request of the general practitioner, was 8.15 x 103 with 85% neutrophils and platelet count was 120,000 mm3. She had right hypochondrial tenderness with just palpable liver on day 5. ALT and AST were 16 mEq/L and 69.7 mEq/L, respectively, on day 3 and they increased to 29.7 mEq/L and 122.2 mEq/L on day 5. Initial C-reactive protein was 6 mg/dL and remained normal. She was monitored for vital signs including urine output and packed cell volume (PCV). Baseline PCV was 32 and the highest noted was 35. The lowest platelet count documented was 67,000/mm3 and the lowest WBC count was 2.27 x 103. She did not show signs of fluid leakage. However, there was a second episode of gum bleeding on day 5 with normal clotting profile (INR: 1.1 and APTT: 35). She was positive for IgM and negative for IgG antibodies for dengue virus.
On the 5th day of illness, she developed tremors in her upper limbs. She had cogwheel rigidity, mask like face, and staccato speech. Power was grade four in all four limbs with normal reflexes. CT scan of brain revealed diffuse hypodense areas in bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus with predominant involvement of right side (Figure 2). During the first 48 hours after the onset of neurological symptoms, she showed rapid deterioration and became aphasic with severe paucity of movements. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 2 lymphocytes without any polymorphs and normal proteins. She recovered dramatically and showed complete recovery within 3 weeks after onset of illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, and gingival bleeding, followed on day 5 by acute parkinsonism and aphasia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy toddler presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, and gum bleeding on day 1 (recurring on day 5). On day 5 of illness, she developed upper-limb tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like facies, and staccato speech, progressing over 48 hours to aphasia and severe akinesia/bradykinesia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy child with no significant past illnesses.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, gum bleeding (days 1 and 5), upper-limb tremors, mask-like facies, staccato speech/aphasia, and paucity of movement.

objective.physical_examination: No signs of plasma leakage; right hypochondrial tenderness with a just-palpable liver on day 5. Neurological exam on day 5 revealed upper-limb tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like facies, staccato speech, grade 4/5 motor power in all four limbs, and normal deep tendon reflexes, progressing over 48 hours to aphasia and severe paucity of movement.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 2 WBC 8.15 x 10^3/mm3 (85% neutrophils; nadir 2.27 x 10^3/mm3) and platelets 120,000/mm3 (nadir 67,000/mm3). Baseline PCV 32% (peak 35%). ALT and AST rose from 16 and 69.7 mEq/L on day 3 to 29.7 and 122.2 mEq/L on day 5. CRP remained normal (6 mg/dL), and day-5 coagulation profile was normal (INR 1.1, aPTT 35 s).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT demonstrated diffuse hypodense areas in the bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus (right > left). CSF analysis showed 2 lymphocytes/mm3, 0 polymorphs, and normal protein.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary dengue encephalitis presenting with acute parkinsonism (tremor, cogwheel rigidity, hypomimia, bradykinesia, and speech arrest) and bilateral basal ganglia/thalamic lesions on brain CT, confirmed by positive dengue IgM and negative dengue IgG serology. Managed supportively with vital sign, urine output, and PCV monitoring, achieving dramatic and complete neurological recovery within 3 weeks of illness onset.
